definition:
Holiness is what makes God God. To call him holy is to say that he is set apart from everything he has made: not one more power inside the world, but its Maker and Lord, unapproachable in majesty and spotless in purity. In Scripture that holiness is never a cold distance. The Holy One comes near, speaks, rescues, and dwells among a people, and he makes them holy so that they can belong to him. Things, places, times, and people are called holy when they are claimed for him and set aside for his use: the seventh day, the ground at the burning bush, the tabernacle and its vessels, the priests, and finally the whole nation. So the Bible's long teaching about altars, sacrifices, purity, priests, and feasts answers one question: how can sinful people live near a holy God and not be destroyed? Its answer reaches beyond ritual. The prophets insist that the God who is holy is known by justice, and that worship without mercy is an offense to him. This study traces God's holiness and the ordered worship through which Israel lived near him. The believer's lifelong growth in holiness has its own study (sanctification), as do God's dwelling place (temple), his radiant presence (glory), and worship more broadly.

The Hebrew root is qadash. The adjective qadosh means ‘holy’, the noun qodesh means ‘holiness’ or ‘a holy thing’ (and, with the article, ‘the holy place’), and the verb in its various stems means ‘to be holy’, ‘to consecrate’, or ‘to treat as holy’. The root's origin is uncertain. Some scholars have connected it with cutting or separation, others with brightness, and neither guess should decide its meaning; usage does. Leviticus gives the grid in which the word works: the priests are to “distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean” (Leviticus 10:10). ‘Common’ (chol) is the ordinary state of things, not something bad. ‘Clean’ (tahor) and ‘unclean’ (tame’) describe fitness to approach the sanctuary. Holiness is the positive pole: what belongs to God. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, rendered qadosh chiefly with hagios, and the New Testament builds its vocabulary on that word: hagios (‘holy’, and as a plural noun hoi hagioi, ‘the holy ones’ or ‘saints’), hagiazō (‘to sanctify’ or ‘to hallow’), hagiasmos (‘sanctification’ or ‘holiness’), and hagiōsynē (‘holiness’ as a quality). The word hosios, ‘devout’ or ‘holy’, appears less often and is used of Jesus as God's ‘Holy One’ in Acts 2:27, quoting Psalm 16:10.
ot:
The first thing Scripture calls holy is not a place or a person but a day. God “blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (Genesis 2:3), and time itself is claimed for him before any altar is built. The word does not appear again until Moses stands before the burning bush and hears, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). Holiness there is not a property of the soil but the nearness of God. After the Red Sea Israel sings the first hymn to God's holiness: “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD? Who is like You—majestic in holiness” (Exodus 15:11). At Sinai the whole nation is summoned into that nearness. God reminds them of rescue and then declares that they will be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), yet the same chapter sets limits around the mountain lest the people break through and die (19:12, 21-24). That double movement, invitation and boundary, shapes everything that follows.

The tabernacle and Leviticus turn the double movement into a way of life. The sanctuary was arranged in rising degrees of holiness: the camp, the courtyard with its altar, the Holy Place with its lampstand, table, and incense altar, and the Most Holy Place where the ark stood beneath the cherubim. The high priest wore a gold plate engraved “HOLY TO THE LORD” (Exodus 28:36), and only he entered the inner room, once a year (Leviticus 16:2). The sacrifices of Leviticus 1 to 7 (burnt, grain, peace, purification, and reparation offerings) gave Israel ways to approach God, give thanks, share a meal before him, and deal with sin, because “it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul” (Leviticus 17:11). The danger was real. When Nadab and Abihu offered “unauthorized fire before the LORD,” fire came out and consumed them, and Moses told Aaron that God had said, “To those who come near Me I will show My holiness” (Leviticus 10:1-3). The purity laws that follow (Leviticus 11 to 15) concern food, childbirth, skin disease, bodily discharges, and contact with the dead. Uncleanness in these chapters is not sin. A mother after childbirth and a son who buries his father are unclean without having done wrong. Uncleanness is a condition that must not be brought into contact with the holy, and most of it passes with time and washing. Jacob Milgrom's commentary on Leviticus (Anchor Bible, three volumes, 1991 to 2001) argued that the common thread is death, so that the system taught Israel that the holy God is the God of life. The Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) cleansed the sanctuary itself from the people's impurities and sins so that God could go on dwelling among them.

Leviticus never lets holiness shrink to ritual. Its refrain, “be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44-45), grounds the call in God's own character and in the exodus: “I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt so that I would be your God.” The chapters scholars have called the Holiness Code since August Klostermann named them in 1877 (Leviticus 17 to 26) open their central chapter with “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (19:2) and then define holiness as honoring parents, leaving the edges of the harvest “for the poor and the foreigner” (19:10), paying wages on the day they are earned, judging fairly, and loving the neighbor and the foreigner as oneself (19:18, 34). God is also the one who makes Israel holy: “I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (20:8), “I have set you apart from the nations to be My own” (20:26). The calendar made time holy as well. Leviticus 23 lists “the feasts of the LORD that you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies” (23:2), from the weekly Sabbath and Passover to the Day of Atonement and Tabernacles. Three times a year Israel's men were to appear before the LORD at the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 16:16), so that the rhythm of the year kept retelling rescue, harvest, forgiveness, and wilderness dependence.

The histories show the fearsomeness of God's holiness and the mercy within it. When the ark was mishandled at Beth-shemesh the survivors asked, “Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?” (1 Samuel 6:20), and Uzzah died when he took hold of the ark on the road to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:6-7). Joshua warned the people that they could not serve the LORD lightly, “for He is a holy God” (Joshua 24:19). The Psalms answer the question of who may approach: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:4). Psalm 99 cries three times that God is holy, and joins that holiness to justice (“The mighty King loves justice,” 99:4) and to forgiveness (“You were a forgiving God to them,” 99:8). Israel is called to “worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness” (Psalm 96:9).

The prophets deepen everything. In the year King Uzziah died (around 740 BC), Isaiah saw the Lord enthroned and heard the seraphim call, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3). Hebrew often repeats a word for emphasis, and the threefold form is the strongest the language offers. Isaiah's response was not wonder but ruin, “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips” (6:5), and his cleansing came from the altar before his commission. From then on his favorite name for God is ‘the Holy One of Israel’, used about twenty-five times in the book and only a handful elsewhere. The title holds together judgment on a people who “have despised the Holy One of Israel” (1:4) and comfort: “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel” (41:14). God's holiness is moral: “the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness” (5:16). So the prophets condemn worship that leaves injustice untouched. Isaiah hears God reject sacrifices and Sabbaths from hands “covered with blood” and command, “seek justice and correct the oppressor” (Isaiah 1:11-17). Amos hears, “I hate, I despise your feasts,” and, “let justice roll on like a river” (Amos 5:21-24). Micah answers the worshiper's question with “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8), and Hosea hears, “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). Nineteenth-century critics often read these texts as the prophets rejecting the cult altogether; most interpreters now read them as rejecting worship emptied of obedience, since the same prophets expect a purified temple and offerings. Holiness is also the ground of mercy. In Hosea God refuses to destroy Ephraim, “For I am God and not man— the Holy One among you” (Hosea 11:9), and in Isaiah the one “whose name is Holy” dwells “with the oppressed and humble in spirit” (Isaiah 57:15). Ezekiel promises that God will act “for My holy name,” cleansing his people and putting his Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:22-27). Zechariah closes with a picture of holiness spilling over its boundaries until “HOLY TO THE LORD” is written on the bells of horses and “every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy” (Zechariah 14:20-21).
nt:
The New Testament confesses Jesus as the Holy One in person. The angel tells Mary that “the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35), and Mary sings, “Holy is His name” (1:49). An unclean spirit in the Capernaum synagogue shrieks, “I know who You are—the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24), and Peter confesses the same after the hard teaching in John 6: “We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God” (John 6:69). After the great catch of fish Peter reacts as Isaiah did in the temple: “Go away from me,” he tells Jesus, “for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8). In Acts the apostles charge Jerusalem with having “rejected the Holy and Righteous One” (Acts 3:14). The first Christians confessed Jesus as Lord, and the church's creeds later confessed him as true God. When they called him the Holy One they were saying what the Old Testament said of the LORD.

What Jesus did with that holiness is new. Under the law, holiness did not spread by touch but impurity did; the priests told Haggai that consecrated meat does not make other food holy, while one defiled by a corpse defiles what he touches (Haggai 2:12-13). Jesus reverses the direction. He touches a man with a skin disease and says, “Be clean” (Mark 1:41). A woman who had been bleeding for twelve years, and so would have been unclean for all that time (Leviticus 15:25), touches his cloak and is healed, and he calls her “Daughter” (Mark 5:25-34). Minutes later he takes a dead girl by the hand and raises her (5:41). In him cleanness is contagious. He teaches that what defiles is what comes from the heart, and Mark notes, “(Thus all foods are clean.)” (Mark 7:15-19); Peter later learns the same in a vision, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15). Jesus also takes up the prophets' critique. Twice in Matthew he quotes Hosea's “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). He teaches his disciples to pray first, “hallowed be Your name” (Matthew 6:9), which asks God to do what he promised in Ezekiel 36: to show his name holy. On the night before his death he prays, “For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth” (John 17:19), offering himself as the consecrated sacrifice. The torn temple curtain at his death (Mark 15:38) and Hebrews' teaching that “we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10) show the way into God's holy presence opened by his death.

The apostles apply Israel's holiness vocabulary to the church. Paul addresses a quarrelsome congregation as “those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy” (1 Corinthians 1:2), and ‘saints’ (hoi hagioi) is the New Testament's ordinary word for believers, not a title for a spiritual elite. Their holiness is first a gift, since “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 6:11), and then a calling worked out in the body, especially in sexual faithfulness and in not wronging a brother (1 Thessalonians 4:3-7). Peter quotes Leviticus directly: “Be holy, because I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16), and gives the church Israel's Sinai titles, “a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). Worship is redefined without being made smaller: Paul urges believers “to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship” (Romans 12:1), where the Greek logikē latreia can mean ‘spiritual’ or ‘reasonable’ worship. Hebrews calls believers to pursue “holiness, without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14), and says God disciplines his children “so that we may share in His holiness” (12:10). The Spirit whom Christ gives is himself named Holy, and the church's holiness is his work (the study on sanctification traces it in detail).

Revelation closes the canon with Isaiah's vision reopened. The living creatures around the throne never stop saying, “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come” (Revelation 4:8), and the song of the redeemed asks, “Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy” (15:4), expecting that all nations will come and worship. The holy city needs no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple (21:22), and “nothing unclean will ever enter it” (21:27). The graded boundaries of the tabernacle are gone not because holiness has been relaxed but because it has filled everything, as Zechariah foresaw. The Holy One who kept Israel at a distance with limits around the mountain ends by giving his people his face (22:4).

keyTexts.why: The first time Scripture calls a place holy: the ground is holy because God is present, and Moses must remove his sandals and hide his face.
God calls the rescued nation to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, while boundaries around the mountain guard the people from his holiness.
The death of Nadab and Abihu shows the danger of approaching God on one's own terms, and the priests are charged to distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean.
The refrain ‘be holy, because I am holy’, grounded both in God's character and in the exodus, later quoted in 1 Peter 1:16.
Holiness defined as family honor, care for the poor and the foreigner, honest dealing, fair courts, and love of neighbor, not ritual alone.
Three times the psalm cries that God is holy, and it joins his holiness to justice, to answered prayer, and to forgiveness.
The seraphim's threefold ‘holy’, the prophet's sense of ruin, his cleansing from the altar, and his commission: the Bible's central vision of God's holiness.
God's holiness is the reason he does not destroy Ephraim: because he is God and not man, the Holy One among them, he will not come in wrath.
God rejects feasts and offerings from people who trample justice, the sharpest prophetic statement that worship reaches into justice.
God will show his holy name by cleansing his people, giving them a new heart, and putting his Spirit within them.
In the last day holiness spills over every boundary, down to the horses' bells and the cooking pots.
Jesus is touched by an unclean woman and takes a dead girl by the hand, and instead of being defiled he makes them clean and whole.
Believers offer their bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, so that worship reaches every part of life.
Peter applies Leviticus to the church: as the one who called them is holy, they are to be holy in all they do.
The heavenly worship takes up Isaiah's threefold ‘holy’ and joins it to praise of God as Creator.

history:
The early church's worship carried Isaiah's vision at its center. By the fourth century the eucharistic prayers of East and West led the congregation into the seraphim's song, the Sanctus; the Mystagogical Catecheses attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem (5.6, late fourth century) describe it, explaining that the church joins the praise of the angels. The Te Deum, a Latin hymn from about the same period, gives it a place as well. The Eastern churches also sang the Trisagion (‘thrice holy’), a hymn addressing God as holy, mighty, and immortal; the acts of the Council of Chalcedon (451) record it being sung. When Peter the Fuller, patriarch of Antioch in the 470s and 480s, added the words ‘who was crucified for us’, a long dispute followed over whether the hymn addressed the Trinity or Christ alone, and an attempt to use the expanded form at Constantinople in 512 set off a riot. Early Christian writers often heard in Isaiah's threefold ‘holy’ a hint of the Trinity, a reading most modern interpreters treat as a Christian re-reading of what is in Hebrew a form of emphasis. The Second Council of Nicaea (787), in defending the use of icons, distinguished the honor that may be given to holy images and saints from the worship (latreia) that belongs to God alone. In the West, Thomas Aquinas treated religion, the giving of due worship to God, as a moral virtue belonging to justice (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 81, about 1270). Jewish interpretation developed along its own line; Rashi, commenting on Leviticus 19:2, took the command to be holy to mean keeping apart from forbidden sexual unions, following earlier rabbinic readings.

The Reformation challenged the medieval map of holiness. Luther's address To the Christian Nobility (1520) argued that all the baptized are consecrated priests, and his teaching on vocation declared that a farmer or a mother serves God as truly as a monk. Calvin opened his Institutes by joining the knowledge of God and the knowledge of self, and cited the terror of Isaiah and others before God's majesty as proof that people only see themselves truly when they have seen God (Institutes 1.1.3). The Reformed churches drew from God's holiness a strict view of worship: the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 21.1) taught that God may be worshiped only in the ways he has instituted. Lutherans and Anglicans held that the church may order ceremonies not forbidden by Scripture (Augsburg Confession, Article 15, 1530; Thirty-Nine Articles, Articles 20 and 34), and Richard Hooker defended that view in his Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (from 1594). The Wesleyan and later holiness movements placed personal holiness at the center of Christian experience; that story belongs to the study on sanctification. The Second Vatican Council's constitution on the church, Lumen Gentium (1964), devoted its fifth chapter to the universal call of every believer to holiness.

Modern study reopened the subject from several sides. Rudolf Otto's The Idea of the Holy (Das Heilige, 1917) described the holy as the numinous, a mystery that both overwhelms and attracts, and made the word a category of religious experience in general; his critics replied that the Bible's Holy One is not a feeling but a personal God whose holiness is moral. Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics II/1 (1940, section 30), treated holiness together with grace, arguing that God's holiness is the holiness of his love: in seeking fellowship with his creatures God remains Lord, and his love judges and excludes the sin that opposes it. Old Testament scholarship transformed the reading of Leviticus: Gordon Wenham's commentary (1979), Mary Douglas (1966, 1999), Jacob Milgrom (1991 to 2001), and Philip Jenson (1992) showed that the purity system has a coherent theological logic rather than being a collection of taboos. Israel Knohl's The Sanctuary of Silence (1995) argued that the Holiness Code is later than the rest of the priestly law, a view debated among critical scholars. John Webster's Holiness (2003) argued that God's holiness must be understood from the Trinity and his free, gracious relation to his people, and traced it into the life of the church in worship and witness.

differ.body: Because God is holy, sinful people may approach him only in the ways he has appointed, and adding human inventions to worship repeats the error of Nadab and Abihu's unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10:1-3) and of the golden calf, which was made to honor the LORD (Exodus 32:5). Worship should therefore consist of the elements Scripture commands: reading and preaching the word, prayer, singing, the sacraments, and giving. Circumstances such as time and place are ordered by wisdom. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 21) gives the classic statement, and the Scottish and Dutch Reformed traditions practiced it, some churches going so far as to sing only the Psalms.

The church may use in worship whatever Scripture does not forbid, provided it serves the gospel, keeps good order, and edifies. The New Testament gives no complete order of service, and the church has freedom to shape its liturgy, its calendar, its music, and its ceremonies, as long as none of them is imposed as necessary for salvation. The Augsburg Confession (1530, Article 15) and the Thirty-Nine Articles (Articles 20 and 34) teach this, and Richard Hooker defended it at length. Its defenders argue that holiness is honored by beauty and order received from the church's long history, not only by what a single text explicitly commands.

differ.view: The sacramental and liturgical view (Orthodox and Catholic)
differ.body: The church's worship on earth takes part in the worship of heaven, where the angels and the saints already surround God's throne (Hebrews 12:22-24; Revelation 4 and 5). God's holiness is communicated through the incarnate Christ and therefore through material things he has claimed: the sacraments, consecrated places, and holy images, which are honored but never worshiped, as the Second Council of Nicaea (787) taught. The ancient liturgies, such as the Eastern Divine Liturgy and the Roman Mass, are received as the church's inheritance. The Second Vatican Council's constitution on the liturgy, Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), describes the earthly liturgy as a foretaste of the heavenly one.

errors:
The church has rejected distortions of God's holiness on several sides. Marcion (in Rome around 144) divided the just God of the Old Testament from the good Father of Jesus; the church answered that the Holy One of Israel and the Father of Jesus Christ are one God, holy and merciful at once, as Hosea 11:9 already says. A related error treats God's holiness as terror without mercy, so that the sinner can only hide; Isaiah's cleansing coal and Jesus's touch refute it. The opposite error dissolves holiness into a tolerant love that asks nothing, which Scripture refuses in every book, since the one who calls is holy and calls his people to be holy in all they do. Ritualism, the belief that correct worship pleases God whatever the worshiper's life, was the target of the prophets (Isaiah 1; Amos 5), and Jesus renewed their protest.

A second family of errors mislocates holiness. Donatism, a North African movement of the fourth and fifth centuries, held that the holiness of the church and its sacraments depends on the purity of its ministers; Augustine answered that the church is holy because of Christ, whose sacraments remain his even in unworthy hands, and the church has confessed the same since. Separatism treats holiness as withdrawal from contact with sinners, the very thing Jesus was accused of neglecting when he ate with them. Christians have also often caricatured Israel's purity laws as empty legalism, a reading that ignores the law's own concern for justice and its provision of atonement, and that misses how Jesus fulfilled the system rather than despising it.
life:
God's holiness sets the proportions of a human life. It humbles, because no one stands before the Holy One on his own merits, and it comforts, because the Holy One is the one who cleanses lips, heals the unclean, and says “Daughter” to the woman who touched him. A Christian's worship begins there: not with performance, but with coming near through the sacrifice God has provided. It then spreads outward. Scripture never lets worship stay inside the sanctuary. The same chapter that says “be holy” speaks of harvest edges left for the poor, wages paid on time, and fair courts, and Paul calls the offering of the whole body ‘spiritual worship’.

In practice this means that reverence and justice belong together. Prayer that begins “hallowed be Your name” asks God to make his holiness seen, first in the one who prays. Sunday worship, honest business, sexual faithfulness, and care for the stranger are not separate departments of religion but one holiness lived in different rooms. And Christian hope has the shape of Zechariah's cooking pots: a day when nothing ordinary is merely ordinary any more, because everything will belong to God.
questions: Leviticus distinguishes holy from common and clean from unclean, and says uncleanness is not the same as sin. How does that distinction help you read the purity laws, and what does Jesus do with them?
Isaiah responded to God's holiness with ‘Woe is me’, and Hosea says God's holiness is the reason he shows mercy. How do these two passages fit together?
The prophets insist that worship without justice offends God. Where might your own worship, or your church's, be separated from how you treat the poor, the stranger, or the neighbor?
